claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy with minimal platinum-group-metal content.
The initial catalyst has moderate CO and hydrocarbon oxidation activity.
The initial catalyst suffers from poisoning and sintering under low-temperature or transient exhaust conditions.
A new machine-learning computational method identified tungsten as a suitable dopant.
The proposed intervention is addition of less than 5 at.% tungsten to the catalyst.
Tungsten doping will optimize the catalyst's surface composition and structure.
Tungsten doping will cause tungsten or tungsten-oxide species to become enriched at active surface sites.
Surface tungsten species will stabilize the catalyst microstructure and reduce sintering.
Surface tungsten species will create oxygen vacancies beneficial for catalytic reactions.
Tungsten will anchor active sites and enhance oxygen-vacancy formation.
Enhanced oxygen-vacancy formation will facilitate CO and hydrocarbon oxidation at lower temperatures.
The tungsten-mediated surface changes will increase resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
Mitigation of sintering during aging will sustain catalytic activity over a vehicle lifetime.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, tungsten doping will lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperatures and enable effective oxidation below 150 °C.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, tungsten doping will reduce activity loss in the presence of H2O and NO.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, tungsten doping will improve structural stability after accelerated aging.
The intervention will not increase platinum-group-metal content.
The predicted improvements apply under transient, sub-150 °C automotive exhaust, H2O and NO exposure, and accelerated thermal and moisture aging.
The optimal tungsten concentration may be sensitive to small variations in processing.
